utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before we have the witness, there are two administrative matters I would like to announce. The first one is that we are not going to hear any more witnesses after the present witness this afternoon. Which will also mean that we have to finish the present witness today, but we are not going to hear any more witnesses this week. The second matter is, as for the next Tuesday's schedule, we will start from 3.30 in the afternoon instead of 2.15 because this courtroom will be used for another proceedings at 2.15. So next Tuesday afternoon, we will have two sittings. Each for 90 minutes. Yes, could we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can you hear me? Of course. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in your military experience as you've described it to us in the past day or two, did you notice this as a matter of what had been JNA military doctrine or practice, this pattern, that what would happen is actions would be taken to alarm the local population, the local population would be armed, then an incident would be created and that incident would be used as a pretext for further action?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a scenario that was -- that started in Croatia and was repeated in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but this was more, I think, of Serb army dominated doctrine than actual JNA doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, the Serb-dominated JNA doctrine and the JNA were, as you told us, largely one and the same thing, weren't they? Because the JNA was Serb-dominated?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And to the extent that there were, I say to the extent, that there were previous professional JNA officers, either Croat or Muslim, it is from the JNA and its military doctrine that they came, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, sir -- actually I know, that doctrine varied in the HVO component and the Muslim component.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I have the usher please show you P904 which is the organisational chart, if you will of the HVO military and the English translation is P904. Perhaps it's just as well if the English version be put on the ELMO, please, P904.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, based on what you have testified to so far, looking at this chart, where would you put the "Convicts Battalion"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned before that it would have been attached either to the Ministry of Defence or at the main headquarters level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, I should ask, and I'm sorry if I've caused some confusion, but Mr. Usher, if you could show him the coloured version as well, the -- it's defence Exhibit D1/82, sir, if the usher can be so kind to it assist you, provide you with a marker, looking at the chart, then, can you mark in the box or however you'd like to do it, an arrow where you would fit the Convicts Battalion on this chart?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, for -- in the English, looking at your markings and then comparing it to P904, you have marked the box that is in English titled HQ or headquarters units, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the box sir, of subordinate units, units directly subordinate to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And when you say headquarters in this instance, just so the record is very clear, are you talking about the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO -- this is a schematic diagram of the HVO head quarters I believe, and the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I just want to be clear, when you say they were directly subordinated to headquarters, who in headquarters are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Chief of Staff or the commander of the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although I mentioned before in my testimony that there were times during the war that units such as the Convicts Battalion, because there were many, not just one, were attached to a sector in the Ministry of Defence called the command for special units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, when was that command established, sir? As best you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say most of the reforms took place in late or mid--- they started in 1993, mid-1993, and continued right until -- for the year, until the beginning of the joints operations against Republika Srpska in the 10th month of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you're telling us that these reforms, various reforms, began in approximately mid-1993, but if I hear you correctly, you cannot give us any more specificity as to what point any sort of central command was put over the so-called "special units"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date for when the exact command relationships changed I'm not too certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you've said just a moment ago that it was not just the Convicts Battalion, there were other such units and again I want to be clear, please, there was a unit called the "Bruno Busic unit," correct, brigade, I'm not sure the force sides but perhaps a brigade, a battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a regiment originally, yes, there was such a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was also another similar unit called the "Ludvig Pavlovic"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And briefly, and I don't want to go too much into this but are there are other similar ones that I haven't named that you would care to name that were similar to those two, Bruno Busic and Ludvig Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were units in the operative zones which performed a similar function.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any units in your operative zone that performed such a function?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a similar unit, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was it called?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an international platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What do you mean by international?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was formed of four nationals that joined the brigade during the course of the conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how was this in some way a special unit, or how do you compare it to the units were you telling us about a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For language purposes, since they came from a variety of western countries, I amalgamated them in one unit and the majority of them were ex-professional soldiers who -- were the ranks from -- ranging from colonel to major NCO or senior NCO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness please break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, looking back at the organisational chart, either one, there are actually two boxes on the upper right part of the chart, the headquarters units which you I believe marked with an "X" to the right of, there is another box immediately above that called "units for special assignments and professional units". Now, how is that different than the box that you marked as headquarters unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I clarified before that during the course of the war, that unit would have been attached to one of the two sectors. The headquarters sector, however, in late 1993, had to it attached also as an asset a communications company, artillery battalion and a logistics battalion. There were other units subordinate to the headquarters but this varied.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me suggest to you, sir, and I'm sure you know more about military charts than I do, but when it says head quarters units here, isn't that in fact meant to indicate what you just said, those were support units, the kind of units needed to run a headquarters staff a logistics component, an administrative component, even a clerical component. Isn't that what's typically referred to it as a headquarters unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, there is a headquarters structure with its five sectors or four sectors, personnel, your headquarters staff, and there were units attached to that headquarters, where assets are grouped at that level, at that high level so they could be used as an asset at lower levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me ask you this, going back to the Bruno Busic and Ludvig Pavlovic units, would you put those in the headquarters unit box or would you put it in the units for special assignments and professional units box?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the outset of the war, I'm fairly certain that they were attached to the then embryonic structure of the Ministry of Defence, but later they were used as a fire-fighting unit, from the -- used by the headquarters, main headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir, so we can move on, can I understand then that what you said in the last few minutes about the Bruno Busic and the Ludvig Pavlovic units would apply equally to the Convicts Battalion? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were used in a similar role.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if the usher could please show you what's been marked very early in the trial as Exhibit P2 which is a map, I think the easiest thing to do, Mr. Usher if we put just one version on the ELMO, you can use this one, if you like, P2. I'm going to focus primarily on the left half of the page, Mr. Usher, and with the video booth or audio booth's assistance if we can -- yes, there we go. I think that's for these purposes fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now in terms of your principal area of responsibility or that is, perhaps I should say your headquarters, to the extent you had one, that you were managed to stay in for any length of time, you've talked about Tomislavgrad. Can you show us on the map where Tomislavgrad is located. If it assists you on this map it's also been called "Duvno"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Duvno.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're pointing. Is that where your principle base of operations was, in the city or town of Duvno, in the municipality of Duvno?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the main headquarters but as the situation changes there were tactical headquarters elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell the Judges when the name was changed from Duvno to Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not too certain but I believe it was during the old Yugoslavia. It was named after -- not King Tomislav that was crowned there, the Croatian king, but after the son of the Yugoslav royal monarch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, is it not true that Duvno was commonly considered an old Muslim name and that Tomislavgrad was considered a Croatian name?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most place names in Bosnia-Herzegovina have two names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So for the purposes of your brigade and your testimony, when the HVO referred to it, they referred to it as Tomislavgrad and not Duvno, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't really pay too much if I can attention to the name. It was called -- I heard it called both terms over the past ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I heard your testimony correctly, sir, you've testified that there were no ATGs in your area of operations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within my command structure, there were no ATGs, that's what I mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honours, but I'd like to hear the foundation for assertion that Duvno is an old Muslim name, as the Prosecution suggests, because the Defence puts it to the Court that it has never been the case, and how can the witness, who has never been -- who is not an expert, and I was objected to because of that, how can the witness be examined about this by the Prosecution? The defence claims that Duvno is definitely not a Muslim name of that town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we have already passed this issue and this name of the town is not the main subject matter of this cross-examination. We will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I believe you said that there were no ATGs in your command structure but I also understood you to say, and perhaps I misheard you, there were no ATGs that you had experience with during the war in 1992 and 1993. Now did I mishear you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not misheard me, maybe you misunderstood me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Did you have experience working with, if you will, fighting along side, ATGs in the time period from late 1992 to early 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are units that come to mind but again, the term ATG may not apply to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, sir, I'll just have to represent to you for purposes of these proceedings that we realise there could be other units of a similar nature, but ATG in this proceeding has particular reference. So my only question to you at the moment is were there any units that you operated with that used that terminology, or that were called an ATG?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an ATG Livno, actually a special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir I'm not sure what you're saying, was it called ATG or are you saying it was a special unit called Livno, please listen to it and answer my question. I'm not asking about special units. I'm asking about units that used the name ATG?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may answer the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, may I ask Your Honours to request from the Prosecutor to perhaps calm down a little, change the tone, because in this case, it has not been yet clearly defined what is an ATG and what is a special unit, and let's have a witnesses clear this up. That is why we are calling witnesses. I do not know at which point in this case it has been clearly establish what was an ATG and what was a special unit, because we were talking that there were units called special purpose units, special units, ATG units. That is why we have been producing evidence all the time in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this moment we would like to hear from the witness to tell us what is the ATG Livno.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the term ATG in my opinion is very loosely used. I've heard other terms. It was not a standardised term in the HVO. There were -- the term more appropriate was the term used in the graphic presentation, [Interpretation] Special purpose units, special assignment units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand that, and you've given your answer. I'm asking you a very specific question. Did you have experience with any unit that in its name, just like the HVO or just like the 1st Brigade or the 115th regiment, did you engage with any units in your experience that used the name in its name the word or indication ATG?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of an ATG group called the "ATG Baja Kraljevic"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In what context did you hear it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were also one of the units, amalgamated into the 2nd Guards Brigade in the beginning, end of 1993, beginning of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was it before it became part of the 2nd Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of the units, one of the smaller units, in the -- in the Mostar zone that were amalgamated in the 2nd Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Whether it was in the Mostar zone what larger unit was it a part of?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought they were an individual unit named after the name itself, is a connotation to a member killed during the taking of the Mostar barracks so they were formed I would again presume, from people from Mostar in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you not hear, sir, that that ATG Baja Kraljevic was part of the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that fact, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of an ATG called either the "Mrmak" or "Vinko Skrobo ATG"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directly what I heard in dispatches or after the conflict in 1994. I believe there were individuals also amalgamated into the 2nd Guards Brigade from those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where did that unit operate in 1993, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe in the Mostar area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of that unit was?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- I've never individually met him. I heard that it was a Mr. Stela. I don't know. This was in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going back to these special units of the type that we were talking about earlier, the ones on the organisational chart, the Convicts Battalion, the Bruno Busic, the Ante Pavlovic, during any time that you and your unit was engaged in fighting in 1993, and I'm now referring specifically to the calendar year 1993, did you ever have occasion to request the assistance or, to use a word that seems often used in connection with these units, the "intervention" of one of those units?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, sir, is it fair to say that you have nothing to tell this Chamber in terms of firsthand knowledge about how such one of those units would be called up and put into action, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I earlier explained the process of requesting an asset from higher headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But you yourself, during 1993, never engaged in that process yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that time period, my brigade held a static position or the position shifted over the months but there was no need to request assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps in that regard, sir, before we put the map P2 away could you show us where this position primarily was? Can you point to the place on the map, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which date are we referring to, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You just told us this during most of 1993, were you in a quote "static position," so can you show us that position?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of the brigade held a position towards Jablanica and it's not too well shown on the map, but it would be to the north west of Jablanica from approximately the village of Kucani, which is not on the map, and that was on the left and on the right Strop, which goes through -- it crossed -- the position mainly crossed the main road of Jablanica Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir with a pointer, I don't know if perhaps the pointer is too broad, but you were pointing in the are of Sovici Doljani. Now did your position encompass Sovici Doljani?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It encompassed Doljani, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In what time period was that the case? By that I mean, sir, beginning point when that was your area of responsibilities and the end point if there was one?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been towards the end of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you started?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the position was set, when we -- the position shifted slightly but we basically took over the defence from the Rama Brigade on the left side and the Mijat Tomic and Siroki Brijeg unit on the right who held the position from -- in the valley of Doljani from Ilijin Grude to Strop, which is basically across the canyon in which Doljani is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was the end point, if you will, of that assignment? When did you stop holding a position in that area?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were basically there, although other units were detached to, on the Uskoplje front, but we were basically there until the second month of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And where was your headquarters, your personal base of operations, during that time period?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My tactical headquarters was in the village of Gracac, which is not on the map, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You've mentioned a couple of other places so I'd like to cover that before we go on. You said the Rama Brigade a few moments ago. Now, is Rama again, another name for what's also called Prozor?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was actually a unit from the Prozor Brigade, a battalion. Actually two oversized companies, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, is it also correct again that Rama, as opposed to Prozor, Rama was the preferred Croatian name?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I -- if -- not to be insolent, I paid more attention to troops on the ground than to place names from what I know, Rama and surroundings were Croatian, Catholic majority for centuries since the 9th century at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You've also mentioned in the last few minutes and in fact yesterday, Uskoplje. Now the Chamber has heard quite a bit of testimony about another place called Gornji Vakuf. Is Uskoplje the Croat name for Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Your Honours Gornji Vakuf is not on this particular map, just to avoid any confusion. It would be roughly just north of the Prozor municipality on the map. Did you ever have any dealings or experience with a Minister of Defence Bruno Stojic during your military activities from late 1992 to early 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Mr. Stojic once, in any detail. We had there was one only longer meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was that meeting about, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in Mostar in the summer of 1992, where I paid a visit to Mr. Stojic with Mr. Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir, it may just be a misunderstanding the parameters of the question I gave a moment ago was between late 1992 and early 1994, I believe, unless I misspoke, so when you say you met with him in the summer of 1992, did you mean to say summer of 1993 or are you just going back to an earlier time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My official business with Mr. Stojic or unofficial, I've only met him at any length personally once.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was the occasion again of that meeting? What was it about?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we wanted to coordinate the zone which was being formed in Tomislavgrad so we asked for advice and for logistical support.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you actually never answered the question that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You didn't answer the question I tried to clarify so I will come back, the meeting was it in the summer of 1992 or the summer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, sir, in the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. What understanding, if any, did you have of the control and responsibility of Mr. Stojic as the Minister of Defence with the operation of the HVO military units?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew Mr. Stojic was the Minister of Defence. That was his position, but apart from the details in the Ministry of Defence, I'm not familiar with --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, for instance, who would report, who would report or be his direct subordinates, to put it the other way around, to Minister Stojic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the structure, I assume that the commanders would report -- would have -- there would be a synergy between the headquarters and the Ministry of Defence, as in any other organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, then that Mr. Stojic would interface with the HVO Main Staff, the general staff?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- I would assume, again, I say I don't know the -- I don't know what tactical SOP they had for this or how the Ministry of Defence worked, how its sectors were structured.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me move on very quickly. I assure you and the Chamber, but just to make it a bit more concrete, when we have talked about people such as Mr. Praljak and Mr. Petkovic, was it your understanding that those two senior officers would report to Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would have more contact with him than myself, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your experience at your level in, again, focusing -- I can tell you, sir that I'm focusing my questions primarily on the time frame late 1992 to early 1994, if that can just assist you or focus you. During that time period, was there a regular reporting mechanism that you followed or practised? Did you have to write any sort of regular, that is daily, weekly, regular reports to any superior that you were -- who you were responsible to?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I avoided paper work as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Don't be a lawyer, sir, to avoid paper work.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was -- no, there is a standard, there is an unwritten SOP in any army which says that no one reads anything longer than two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, so that was your rule in writing reports and now my question to you is what kind of reports did you write?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports I wrote were mainly sent after an action, an ammo and casualty report and a situation report. The internal reporting system within my brigade was based on personal contact between me and my battalion commanders, and the majority of the time it was based -- not the reporting, I should say, but instructions were based on the standard five-paragraph field order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me approach it perhaps from a slightly different angle. Who was your immediate superior during this time period, from late 1992 to early 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been Mr. Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was it Mr. Siljeg's practice to require regular periodic reports from you and other units? Did you have to do a daily report, a weekly report?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a briefing, almost on a nightly basis, on a regular basis, at the -- the tactical headquarters of the zone in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who did Mr. Siljeg, by the way, who did he report to?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be logical he reported to the main headquarters in Mostar wherever they were located at the time, I believe in Posusje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again to be a bit more concrete, at least for instance August 1993, you're saying that to your knowledge, Mr. Siljeg would have reported to Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak or Mr. Petkovic or whoever was in a position of leading the -- being the Chief of Staff at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a few questions about communications which have come up in the trial at one time or another. What kind of field communications did you have available to you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my zone, we were fairly well equipped with field telephones and wire, because there was a cable factory in the town of Tomislavgrad. We used radio to an absolute minimum because it was an unsure means of communication and it was rudimentary and it was a security issue. So we used it to an absolute minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have something in the field that was known as a -- sometimes called a "packet communication"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you describe what that is to the Judges, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a radio relay system between the zones and the main headquarters, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How did it function, just how do you operate a packet communication?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The message is sent and received at the other end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are you talking about voice communications or written communications or what types of communications?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a voice communication which is later translated into the written.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, and again, how does that work, then, if it's sent by voice and then how does it get transformed into a written communication or the written document?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The RTO takes the message puts it in his logbook and writes the message down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What's RTO?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radio telephone operator. And he takes the message to whomever it was sent to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then what happens at the other end?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would be a confirmation that the message had been received and depending on the headquarters, there is usually -- there is a number by which it is registered, there is a stamp designated the headquarters and it is logged either the -- depending what level it was received at, the zone headquarters or the higher headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what -- at the other end at the receiving end, so to speak, is it once again converted from a voice message or a written message to text?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same procedure would follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Assuming, sir, assuming, then, that the operators follow the procedure that you just discussed, it would not be unusual to have one form of a message written in one hand at one end and another -- sorry, Judge Diarra, I'll try to slow down. And another version of roughly very similar, the same content, perhaps, in another hand, and a record at the other end; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again it depends on the type of correspondence, I think or actually depends on the type of correspondence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was there another type of communication that was perhaps -- that operated something along of what might be called a field fax or a telecopy, a telefax type of apparatus?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes there was, there were fax machines in some of the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was it just called a fax machine or was there some other military jargon or word customarily used in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time the time period you're speaking of we had just the ordinary fax machines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the usher could please provide you with Exhibit P299.2, it should be in the bundle of exhibits that were prepared for this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Are you sure, Mr. Scott, it's 299?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I've just been told, perhaps it was added later, but yes, it should be -- or distributed, P, there is actually there may be -- yes, I think so, Judge Clark, 299.2. Perhaps it's loose, sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like you to do, sir, looking at the what we call the B/C/S original, as opposed to the English translation, looking at that document, sir, the form of it and what you see on that sheet of paper, now, what kind of a document or, excuse me, communication would you call that, along the lines we have been talking for a few minutes now?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks to me like a photocopy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of a typed -- of a typed report or a -- it's a copy of a communication from -- from the defence -- defence organ from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me direct your attention. For the moment, I'm going to refer to, even though we can't all -- most of us, or some of us at least, can't read the B/C/S version -- so I'm going to refer for the moment to the original. You see the box roughly in the middle of the page on the right side it starts the very first entry in the upper left corner of the box appears to be "ECV." You see what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And so what is that box all about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would only request this is a new document, I don't know what the source of this document is, and in particular what -- and also what surprises me there is no source of the Zagreb archive, and particularly what surprises me is what has been added by hand in the B/C/S version, you can see that Travnik has been entered by hand, upside down. And that is why I'd be really interested in knowing the -- what is the source and the origin of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think during the cross-examination, the Prosecutor will tell us some information about the sources of this document. Let's continue with this question. What is that "ECV" mean in that box?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's either the sending or the receiving organ, the abbreviation is not familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, all right. Let's go to the next line down, not to the right but next line down appears to have the words, perhaps, Predete, but in any event that's the line I'm referring to and to the rights of that, there is a handwritten number. Can you tell the Judges what that number would indicate?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That again, I assume, is the number of the receiving fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or receiving organ where it was sent, the number where this message was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the next line below that, to your knowledge, what does that information, particularly the part written in, what does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date and the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The next line that starts TLP, what information is meant to be indicated by that line?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The type of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What would a "TLP" be?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Telephone, telegraph, or the radio, there was pocket, meaning the radio which is circled here, written.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How about RRV to the right of the written packet?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the radio communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And ZV?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is wire communications, meaning field phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how about the next item, the last in that row, what would that indicate?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A signature of the individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, before we get to the next line, the end of that row of initials, there is one after ZV and what is that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my copy, it's a little illegible here. I'm not too sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then you began to tell us below that those series of letters or acronyms -- what is meant or indicated below that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the individual, I assume again, the signature of the individual that received the message.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And so far as you can tell us, then, sir, is this a document, is this a fax communication of the type that you told us existed a moment or two ago or some other type? That's my question?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communique to me looks like a fax, a copy of a faxed message.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, before I forget and I don't think it's critical the content of the document itself, what's above it I haven't even asked the witness about because I was interested in the form of the document, but so the record is clear, this is a seized document, seized by the Office of the Prosecutor in an investigation in Vitez of the sort that Mr. Von Hecke testified to in the beginning days of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this document admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I believe it's a new document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as a military man you're familiar with the term or terms or phrase perhaps, I should say, "rules of engagement"?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the term.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you, in your own unit, put any rules of engagement into effect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to ask if you could ask what does the number Z 658.2 mean on this document we were just referring to a bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I thought we had passed this issue already. Is that of crucial importance to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: It's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I better tell you it's the Exhibit number of this document when it was admitted into evidence in the Kordic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have rules of engagement in your unit, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This may be take a little longer to answer if you permit me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My first question is not to explain what they were. Did you have something called rules of conduct. I think that can be answered yes or no. Did you have rules of engagement in your unit, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules of engagement are contained in doctrinal material.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did your unit follow them or not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge and to the best of my capability as a commander I tried to reinforce the so-called rules of engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is yes?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with a written tactical with a written SO -- written individual skills manual, a written individual skills manual and this was underlined at every briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your unit, sir, did you have any rules of engagement dealing with the burning of houses?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the burning of houses is not only a humanitarian -- breaking of humanitarian and international law, it is also tactically unwise because it gives the enemy a target reference point, so for both reasons, this was -- this is strongly opposed in my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you do, sir, if one of your soldiers burned a house, Muslim or Croat, if one of your soldiers burned a house, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never individually, with my own eyes, saw a member of my unit burn a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that because, sir, you'd made it very clear that that conduct would not be tolerated?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are other reasons for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question -- answer my question, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I explained before I had good work I had people that were experienced, that had leadership capabilities. I could not be everywhere at once but my subordinates, my subordinates relayed my intentions successfully, I like to believe, to my soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, was it a rule of conduct in your unit that houses were not to be torched?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was clearly understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What disciplinary measures did you follow with soldiers in your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the offence dictated the punishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Given us some examples, please.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, if someone did not show up for muster at the appropriate assembly area, at the appropriate time, if he did not want to carry a rifle, he carried a shovel, or went on mine-laying detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry went on what detail?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mine-laying detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why would you consider that a disciplinary measure?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was more effective than jailing someone, especially when men were needed, and it was not practical always to -- when we had no clear-cut guidelines or a system of military law, it was more pragmatic and it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I understand your answer to be why that was a substitute or alternative, if you will, for a -- perhaps a trip to the brig, but my question to you is why would being engaged in laying mines be considered a disciplinary measure? Is it more dangerous?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is high risk operation, also digging a defensive line is also not a high risk operation, so to speak, but it's effective.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that was one example. Other examples of disciplinary measures that you took in your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes there is a -- sometimes in extreme measures, in extreme measures, and this was rarely, you would revert to wall to wall counselling.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Meaning?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meaning the Legion way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Meaning?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a NCO has a problem with a subordinate, the problem is solved in a physical manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, that indeed you, in fact, caught one of your soldiers burning a house once and you beat him physically?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've had numerous altercations, not as a bully, but as for -- as for burning a house, I don't recall any one of my soldiers ever burning a house. I remember one, if I can clarify the incident which I think you're speaking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you wish me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on the line almost regularly for years and I walked the ground, I know every rock from -- in every area of operations and zone of interest where my units were employed. So I saw an individual on a roof with a hammer, breaking tiles on the roof, so I asked him what his intention was and he was clearly intoxicated and his answer was, "You said not to burn the house." So that -- maybe that was that incident that you're speaking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what did you do to this soldier, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Went into a room, closed the door and solved it in the Legion way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you find that to be an effective form of discipline?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I think, if I may use a Chinese proverb, which says there is no medicine for a fool except one, sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll have to caution you, sir, because we have a President here who may know more about Chinese proverbs than the rest of us.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told it was a Chinese proverb and if not I excuse myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I never heard of that, but I heard the first one you used. Yeah, there was such a Chinese proverb, but not this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in your military training and experience, did you ever receive training and education in the law of war?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, but it was a quarter of a century ago in the Canadian army, and my memory of the details were somewhat clouded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At any time, sir, during your service in the army of the Republic of Croatia, that is the HV army, did you receive any training or education in the law of war, such as the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no formal training along the line of the Geneva Conventions, but my zone commander Zeljko Siljeg at numerous briefings underlined the proper way to behave, the soldierly way to behave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it your impression, sir, from that that Mr. Siljeg, whatever his rank at the time was, and I don't mean discourtesy, Colonel Siljeg, perhaps, that he was familiar with and knew at least to some degree, the laws of war, including the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume he did because I believe the JNA was a signer or signed the Geneva accords, and he was an ex-member of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you the same question or similar question to what I asked you a moment ago specifically in connection with the HV. When you transferred your services to the HVO, at any time during your -- well, strike that. Not any time but during the time of 1992 to early 1994, did you receive any training in the law of war or humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No formal training, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well I'm going to clarify, sir, you've qualified your answer twice by saying no formal training. Did you receive some sort of training that wasn't formal?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, instructions were given and I recall two orders being given, written by, you say Colonel Siljeg, that underlined steps to be taken for proper behaviour that fall under the same category as humanitarian law, which is how to prevent and how to prohibit such behaviour contrary to the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me move up a level or so, sir, if I can. Did you ever have any experience or knowledge during the war that either Mr. Praljak, General Praljak or General Petkovic had training or knowledge in the laws and customs of war?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would assume that Mr. Petkovic, who was an ex-JNA officer, he in all probability had such training. As for Mr. Praljak, I think -- I don't think he had an extensive military background. I would assume that his was -- his knowledge was minimal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you assist us, sir, and I don't want to be oversimplistic about this, but can you assist us by indicating how much does the law and customs of war vary from what many of us would consider common sense morality?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I basically, the human being that you are, depends on your upbringing. That's maybe an a difficult -- not the answer you're looking for, but standards of behaviour worldwide are standardised, I believe, proper behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you consider covered by, if you will, if I can just use the shorthand phrase, I don't mean it to be anything technical, a common sense rule of war is that you do not kill civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only it's not only a law, I think it's a humanitarian -- it's a -- the word I'm looking for escapes me, but it's common sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, moving on to another topic, you testified, I believe yesterday, that you did not know of any HVO political or military plans to engage in ethnic cleansing in April, 1993. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that in my previous -- yesterday's statement and I still say, and the two main components for such an operation would be mission and intent, and I never verbally or written or in a written order received such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges whether at any time in the first half of April, 1993, were you present or engaged in any meetings with the senior Herceg-Bosna leadership?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the time period again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course. In the first half of May -- excuse me, April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I can recall. I -- they were stationed in, I believe, Grude again and I didn't go there until almost after 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the month of May -- excuse me again, April or May, 1993, did you engage in any meetings with, for example, Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Mr. Boban twice in my life. The first time was in prior to the start of hostilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Grude, in the second month of 1992. And the last time I was close to Mr. Boban was whether I was a pall bearer at his funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How did you come to be a pall bearer for Mr. Boban after his death?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked at the time, I'm trying to remember the year that he died. I was asked, and I -- there were other HVO officers there, seven others, I believe, and I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who asked you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think then it was -- I'm trying to remember, it was General Budimir, who was head of the -- he was second in command to General Dudakovic of the Federation Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall who any of the other pall bearers were?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. There was General Nakic or Brigadier Nakic, at the time. There was Brigadier Milic, my second in command of the brigade. There was, I believe, General Curcic. There was General Sopta was there. And that's all I can recall at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would it sound roughly right to you, sir, if I suggest, just so we have some mark in the record, and probably I hope it would be disputed we can establish it in any event, Mr. Boban died sometime in July, 1997?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the date, I presume.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. But going back to the -- Mr. President I see it's about time for a break, if I can just finish this question or so. Going back to the question where we started, sir, during the months of April and May, 1993, you didn't meet with Mr. Boban and you didn't meet with Jadranko Prlic or Bruno Stojic either, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So when you testified yesterday that you did not receive any orders to carry out ethnic cleansing, what you meant to tell this Chamber is that no such orders were given to you, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I think I said before, is that to understand a mission you need to know the intent of a commander two levels up, and to me that would be either General Petkovic or General Praljak or Mr. -- Whoever was a commander of the HVO at the time -- would be the intent would be passed on to the zone headquarters, all four of them. It would be a coordinated action. And other -- am I speaking too quickly here? A third element necessary for any type of action, apart from the two I mentioned, is lateral cooperation. And to my knowledge, in my area, my zone of operations, there was no such lateral cooperation to carry this mission out, this mission of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, before we break, can I just follow up on that specific point, not necessarily in connection with ethnic cleansing, but during your military experience in 1993, did you always know who was giving you support on the left and right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, sir, is the first part of your situation report, which is the first part of your paragraph -- five-paragraph field order, in your situation report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's a good time, if it suits you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, during your military activities in the year 1993, you came to know of the existence of prison or detention camps at the Heliodrom, a place called Dretelj and Gabela, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know of those camps, I learned after 1994, mostly of the details or from newspapers and articles mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said mostly, sir. Are you telling the Chamber that during 1993, you had no knowledge of the existence of those camps?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I was preoccupied with holding a sector and the details of what transpired in the other operative zone, the details were to me for -- the mission, for completing my mission were not vital to my mission accomplishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've given us a reason why perhaps it was not your top priority, but my question remains: Are you telling this Chamber that you have no knowledge of the existence of those camps in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you honestly the first time I heard of the camps, the actual date that I heard the camps mentioned, whether it was television or newspapers, the picture I formed was basically formed by, as I said, the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm raising a matter that we may get into later perhaps, given time and other considerations, but are you saying then that you did not tell representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor at the end of February of this year that you knew it was general knowledge in 1993 that those camps existed and that terrible things were happening there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason I gave -- the reason I'm giving this statement is because I'm speaking of things that I directly know. The reason I did not sign that statement is because for the letter that was presented in the first part of the -- this -- my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, I assure you that we will get to that, but you talked very -- sir, very expansively during your direct examination about things all over the region of Yugoslavia, and I'll ask it this way. Using the same measure of information, the same type of information on which you voiced a number of opinions during your direct examination, based on that same type of information, are you telling this Chamber that you did not know of the existence of the camps and the conduct that was happening there during 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand behind my original statement a few questions ago that I had no direct knowledge of the details in those camps at the time you're speaking of in 1993, and I do not recall the first time that I heard of the camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm looking at your testimony I'm going to suggest to you that you are being very, very careful about what you're saying. You say you had no direct knowledge. Did you have indirect knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I said I'm not too sure of the time or the date. I had knowledge naturally, but the date that I first received the news of the camps, no one ever confronted me with any type of eyewitness testimony or would have any reason to speak to me about those camps in my zone of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, what kind of knowledge naturally did you have?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the knowledge based, as I said, I formulated my opinion of what I read, what I saw on the television the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you read and see? What did you read in the newspapers and see on television?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- the camps existed, physically, there were -- people were interned there, there were human rights abuses, investigations were taken, the details of those abuses or the perpetrators I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'll ask you again, and I promise I'll move on: Didn't you tell the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor in late February of this year, just a few weeks ago, that the camps and the horrible things that were happening in the camps were a matter of common knowledge in 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not think that one can raise the question of a statement which the witness does not recognise as his own, that one cannot take parts of that statement out of the context, seeing that the witness has completely rejected that statement, disowned the statement. And it is still not quite clear how did he make this -- how did he give his statement because yesterday I heard from the Prosecutor that he was interviewed here as a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, if I'm correct, judging on the basis of this paper that I was given yesterday by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we are not going to debate of the nature of this interview. Here we just -- the Prosecution is asking a question. I think the witness has the full right to answer this question or to deny everything he said in that statement, and we also received the document you submitted to us, which is D1/330, which is the letter written by this witness. When we evaluate all the evidence, we will take that into consideration. Yes, Mr. Scott, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you was, just to come back to it a final time, did you not tell representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor a few weeks ago that the existence of these camps, Heliodrom, Dretelj, Gabela, and the horrible things that were happening in those camps, was common knowledge in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I recall saying, sir, and if I may go back to the original witness statement, there were 64 pages in that statement, and I again repeat the majority of what I said was deleted, and for that reason, I refused to sign the statement. What I recall seeing, I will tell you what I recall seeing, I said that such conduct, if it was true was reprehensible and against the law of nature and God.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it likewise the case sir that it was common knowledge that prisoners, Muslim prisoners, were being taken from the Heliodrom and used for forced labour?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I like to base my evidence on direct observation, not on hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, again I'm not going to argue with you, I assure you and I will assure the Chamber I do not intend to argue with you but I do -- I will make -- I will point out to you that I'm asking for you to answer my questions on the same basis, the kinds of information, direct or indirect, that you answered the questions on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as you know, I insisted, and all my questions were directed at the direct knowledge, and that is what this honourable court also insists upon. It was said on numerous occasions that no hearsay or double -- and moreover double hearsay would not be admitted and the witness has repeated, now several times over, that he had no direct knowledge of this, so I see no purpose in trying to drag some answers out of this witness, since he has repeated four times over that he had no knowledge of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we quite understand that the witness said that he was not there, he did not see, and he did not participate anything like this. We understand that. But the question asked in a different way. The question is, is it common knowledge that prisoners, Muslim prisoners were being taken from Heliodrom and used for forced labour. The Prosecution is asking about common knowledge. The witness could agree with the Prosecutor, but he also could deny it that it is common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if it was common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's hear the answer from this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I answer, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, in my zone of operation, in my brigade, at the time it was not common knowledge. It was not a priority topic in my zone of operations or in my unit. And I stand behind what I said in the first several answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me a minute, sir. Sir, I'm looking now at -- [French interpretation coming through]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have some disruptions -- [Wrong translation coming through]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One, two, three.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Usher if I could have your assistance, please? If this could be placed on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe that's D174.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Top right corner of that, is it 1992? Yeah, that's all right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you, during your direct examination gave testimony on a wide range of things far away from your area of operations, and you've told us today, for instance, that you spent most of 1993 in a holding a part of the line around to the west of Jablanica. Now, sir, should these Judges -- are you telling that -- telling us that these Judges should assess all your testimony on the same basis of what you just said now, that if it isn't based on your personal knowledge what you saw and heard with your own eyes and your own ears, then it should be discounted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I shall repeat, look at the transcript. We -- when you said are we going to Mostar? I said that we would not ask him about Mostar as he did not have direct knowledge about it. We -- I said we would be moving to the Neretva operation, and that is why I did not ask about Mostar, because he has no personal knowledge. I think that is fair. And that is why that was the reason that I moved from this in my direct examination and I don't see why the Prosecutor is focusing on it in his cross-examination. We want to hear about the direct experience, participation, of the general, and the causes which brought about, and resulted in the events in Mostar, and resulted in the operation of Neretva 1993 by the Muslims. And I also emphasise that the gentleman -- the witness has -- cannot enlighten us on Mostar because he has no personal experience and personal knowledge on that, and I would kindly ask you to take that into consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, your question is not directly related to what this witness saw and did during that period, so try to rephrase this question another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my original question was directly related to an issue in this case and that is the use of Muslim prisoners to perform forced labour in Mostar, which the Chamber of course has heard extensive knowledge of. I'm putting it to this witness that such practice was well known and common knowledge in 1993. And he has disputed that, saying, "Well, I won't say anything about something I didn't see with my own eyes." I will move on. I told you Mr. President, I wouldn't argue about it and I won't --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you slow down, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- except to respond to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May I finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- simply to explain to Your Honour to answer your question, Mr. President, as to why the relevance of the questions. I think that the Chamber has heard and of course can draw its own ultimate observations is the difference in the answers given in direct examination and the answers given on cross-examination and with that I won't belabour it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object to the type of examination, where we call into generally and commonly known fact, I believe that generally -- commonly known facts will not be here assessed, so it's wrong, I believe, to -- there is no reason to demand and request from the witness to say whether this was something which was common knowledge or not. So if something is common knowledge, it will not be here, the validity of it will not be demanded of it, so I object to this type of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution has promised to move on. We will not spend much more time on that debate at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance in putting before the witness Exhibit P599.4?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is a commendation that was given to several units, including, I believe, your own, on about the 4th of August, 1993, by the Minister of Defence, Bruno Stojic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber for what action or conduct were you and your unit being commended at this time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The direct translation is for courage, combativeness and morale in successful battles in Northern Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it says the number one or the first unit is the King Tomislav Brigade from Tomislavgrad led by Commander Zeljko?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, can you just explain to the Chamber how a commendation like this would come about? And to be more specific, how would the information on which this commendation is based, come to the attention of minister Stojic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in the army there is a common procedure for commending subordinate, so again I can only assume that Zeljko Siljeg commended the brigade for the above-mentioned and passed on the request to the minister, or Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So it would have gone up from your superior, Mr. Siljeg, to Mr. Stojic, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't remember myself writing such a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your unit, did you receive only this one commendation from late 1992 to early 1994, or did you receive other similar commendations or awards?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For that time period, I don't recall, most of the decorations came after the Washington Agreement was signed, when the rank structure crystallised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you proud to receive this commendation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I think pride was -- took second seat to combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In a second seat capacity, were you proud to receive this award?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at it now, I would say I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you think it was justified?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that you knew Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, or knew of him, and really I wasn't sure, so let me ask you now, do you know him as someone -- as a person you know or do you only know of him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, both.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How do you know him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of him from what I've heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My first question was, how do you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us those occasions, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met. The first time I met Mr. Naletilic was at the change of command dinner in Grude that we spoke in any detail. I believe that was when General Blaskic took over from Mr. Petkovic or General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when was the approximate date of that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been the beginning of 1994 or late -- the beginning of 1994, I believe. And previous to that, or after that, I met him in the summer of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct then for us to understand, sir, that prior to early 1994, you had never met the man, Mladen Naletilic, Tuta?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have never -- we never had contact. Bank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 11442 to 11448.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just to be clear, when you say that, sir, I take that to mean not only had you not met him in a face-to-face, eye-to-eye way, but you had not talked to him on the telephone, you had not corresponded with him, you simply had no contact with the man; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO GLASNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to go back to the second part, and you started to say not only did you know him later, but you knew of him. What did you know of him?
